claim: The neuropeptide Drosulfakinin (Dsk) modulates aggression in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Here we found that the neuropeptide Drosulfakinin (Dsk) modulates aggression in Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Knock-out of Dsk reduced aggression.
source: Knock-out of Dsk or Dsk receptor CCKLR-17D1 reduced aggression.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing reduced lunge frequency and prolonged fighting latency in ΔDsk mutants (Figure 1H, I).

claim: Knock-out of Dsk receptor CCKLR-17D1 reduced aggression.
source: Knock-out of Dsk or Dsk receptor CCKLR-17D1 reduced aggression.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing reduced aggression in ΔCCKLR-17D1 mutants (Figure 3C, D).

claim: Activation of Dsk-expressing neurons increased male aggressive behavior.
source: Activation and inactivation of Dsk-expressing neurons increased and decreased male aggressive behavior, respectively.
evidence: Supported by thermogenetic activation experiments using dTRPA1 (Figure 2L-M).

claim: Inactivation of Dsk-expressing neurons decreased male aggressive behavior.
source: Activation and inactivation of Dsk-expressing neurons increased and decreased male aggressive behavior, respectively.
evidence: Supported by TNT and Kir2.1 inactivation experiments (Figure 2H-K).

claim: Dsk-expressing neurons function downstream of a subset of P1 neurons (P1a-splitGAL4) to control fighting behavior.
source: Moreover, data from transsynaptic tracing, electrophysiology and behavioral epistasis reveal that Dsk-expressing neurons function downstream of a subset of P1 neurons (P1a-splitGAL4) to control fighting behavior.
evidence: Supported by trans-Tango tracing, GRASP, electrophysiology, and behavioral epistasis experiments (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: Winners show increased calcium activity in Dsk-expressing neurons.
source: In addition, winners show increased calcium activity in Dsk-expressing neurons.
evidence: Supported by TRIC experiments showing higher signals in winner brains (Figure 6E-H).

claim: Conditional overexpression of Dsk promotes social dominance.
source: Conditional overexpression of Dsk promotes social dominance, suggesting a positive correlation between Dsk signaling and winning effects.
evidence: Supported by RU486-induced Dsk overexpression experiments (Figure 6A-D).

claim: There is a positive correlation between Dsk signaling and winning effects.
source: Conditional overexpression of Dsk promotes social dominance, suggesting a positive correlation between Dsk signaling and winning effects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the conditional overexpression and TRIC experiments.

claim: The mammalian ortholog CCK has been implicated in mammal aggression.
source: The mammalian ortholog CCK has been implicated in mammal aggression, thus our work suggests a conserved neuromodulatory system for the modulation of aggressive behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on CCK in mammals.

claim: The work suggests a conserved neuromodulatory system for the modulation of aggressive behavior.
source: The mammalian ortholog CCK has been implicated in mammal aggression, thus our work suggests a conserved neuromodulatory system for the modulation of aggressive behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between Dsk and CCK functions across species.

claim: Aggression is a common innate behavior in most vertebrate and invertebrate species.
source: Aggression is a common innate behavior in most vertebrate and invertebrate species and a major driving force for natural and sexual selections (Darwin, 1859; Lorenz, 1963).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Darwin and Lorenz.

claim: Aggression is a major driving force for natural and sexual selections.
source: Aggression is a common innate behavior in most vertebrate and invertebrate species and a major driving force for natural and sexual selections (Darwin, 1859; Lorenz, 1963).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Darwin and Lorenz.

claim: Aggression is a critical behavior for defense against conspecifics to obtain food resources and mating partners.
source: It is a critical behavior for defense against conspecifics to obtain food resources and mating partners (Beye et al., 1998; Kravitz and Huber, 2003; Siegel et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Aggressive behavior of fruit flies was first reported by Alfred Sturtevant.
source: Aggressive behavior of fruit flies was first reported by Alfred Sturtevant (Sturtevant, 1915).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila immunoreactivity is detected in the brains of wildtype and ΔDsk/+ but not detected at all in the brain of ΔDsk/ΔDsk.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed that Dsk immunoreactivity is detected in the brains of wildtype and ΔDsk/+ but not detected at all in the brain of ΔDsk/ΔDsk (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Homozygous ΔDsk male mutants showed reduced frequency of lunge.
source: Interestingly, homozygous ΔDsk male mutants showed reduced frequency of lunge (Figure 1H) and wing threat (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and prolonged latency to initiate fighting (Figure 1I), while conditional overexpression of Dsk promoted aggressive behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Homozygous ΔDsk male mutants showed reduced frequency of wing threat.
source: Interestingly, homozygous ΔDsk male mutants showed reduced frequency of lunge (Figure 1H) and wing threat (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and prolonged latency to initiate fighting (Figure 1I), while conditional overexpression of Dsk promoted aggressive behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Homozygous ΔDsk male mutants showed prolonged latency to initiate fighting.
source: Interestingly, homozygous ΔDsk male mutants showed reduced frequency of lunge (Figure 1H) and wing threat (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and prolonged latency to initiate fighting (Figure 1I), while conditional overexpression of Dsk promoted aggressive behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Conditional overexpression of Dsk promoted aggressive behavior.
source: Interestingly, homozygous ΔDsk male mutants showed reduced frequency of lunge (Figure 1H) and wing threat (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and prolonged latency to initiate fighting (Figure 1I), while conditional overexpression of Dsk promoted aggressive behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Female aggression is suppressed in homozygous ΔDsk mutants.
source: Furthermore, female aggression is also suppressed in homozygous ΔDsk mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Video 1), suggesting that Dsk is required for aggressive behavior in both sexes.
evidence: Supported by female aggression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Video 1.

claim: Dsk is required for aggressive behavior in both sexes.
source: Furthermore, female aggression is also suppressed in homozygous ΔDsk mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Video 1), suggesting that Dsk is required for aggressive behavior in both sexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both male and female ΔDsk mutants show reduced aggression.

claim: The ΔDsk mutants do not show defects in courtship behavior.
source: Note that the ΔDsk mutants do not show defects in courtship behavior or locomotion activity, but show increased food intake (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by courtship behavior data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The ΔDsk mutants do not show defects in locomotion activity.
source: Note that the ΔDsk mutants do not show defects in courtship behavior or locomotion activity, but show increased food intake (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by locomotion data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The ΔDsk mutants show increased food intake.
source: Note that the ΔDsk mutants do not show defects in courtship behavior or locomotion activity, but show increased food intake (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by feeding behavior data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: ΔDskGAL4 is a null mutation for Dsk.
source: ΔDskGAL4 is a null mutation for Dsk, as Dsk immunoreactivity is absent in both ΔDskGAL4/ΔDsk hetero-allelic (Figure 1D) and ΔDskGAL4/ΔDskGAL4 homozygotes (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data showing absence of Dsk immunoreactivity in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Dsk immunoreactivity is absent in ΔDskGAL4/ΔDsk hetero-allelic mutants.
source: ΔDskGAL4 is a null mutation for Dsk, as Dsk immunoreactivity is absent in both ΔDskGAL4/ΔDsk hetero-allelic (Figure 1D) and ΔDskGAL4/ΔDskGAL4 homozygotes (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Dsk immunoreactivity is absent in ΔDskGAL4/ΔDskGAL4 homozygotes.
source: ΔDskGAL4 is a null mutation for Dsk, as Dsk immunoreactivity is absent in both ΔDskGAL4/ΔDsk hetero-allelic (Figure 1D) and ΔDskGAL4/ΔDskGAL4 homozygotes (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ΔDskGAL4 driven UAS-Dsk expression was capable of restoring the Dsk immunoreactivity in ΔDskGAL4/ΔDskGAL4 homozygous mutant background.
source: ΔDskGAL4 driven UAS-Dsk expression was capable of restoring the Dsk immunoreactivity in both ΔDskGAL4/ΔDskGAL4 homozygous mutant background (Figure 1F) and ΔDskGAL4/ΔDsk hetero-allelic mutant background (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ΔDskGAL4 driven UAS-Dsk expression was capable of restoring the Dsk immunoreactivity in ΔDskGAL4/ΔDsk hetero-allelic mutant background.
source: ΔDskGAL4 driven UAS-Dsk expression was capable of restoring the Dsk immunoreactivity in both ΔDskGAL4/ΔDskGAL4 homozygous mutant background (Figure 1F) and ΔDskGAL4/ΔDsk hetero-allelic mutant background (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Dsk expression in ΔDskGAL4 neurons restores the aggression levels of ΔDskGAL4/ΔDskGAL4 and ΔDskGAL4/ΔDsk mutants to comparable levels observed in heterozygous controls.
source: As expected, Dsk expression in ΔDskGAL4 neurons restores the aggression levels of ΔDskGAL4/ΔDskGAL4 and ΔDskGAL4/ΔDsk mutants to comparable levels observed in heterozygous controls (Figure 1J and K).
evidence: Supported by behavioral rescue data shown in Figure 1J and K.

claim: Eight neurons, with four neurons in the lateral region (DSK-L) and four neurons in the middle region (DSK-M) were labeled by DskGAL4 driving the expression of UAS-mCD8:GFP in the brain.
source: Eight neurons, with four neurons in the lateral region (DSK-L) and four neurons in the middle region (DSK-M) were labeled by DskGAL4 driving the expression of UAS-mCD8:GFP in the brain, which fully recapitulated the endogenous expression pattern of Dsk in both female and male brains by co-staining experiments (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: DskGAL4 driven UAS-mCD8:GFP expression fully recapitulated the endogenous expression pattern of Dsk in both female and male brains.
source: Eight neurons, with four neurons in the lateral region (DSK-L) and four neurons in the middle region (DSK-M) were labeled by DskGAL4 driving the expression of UAS-mCD8:GFP in the brain, which fully recapitulated the endogenous expression pattern of Dsk in both female and male brains by co-staining experiments (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by co-staining experiments shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Eight DSK-expressing neurons were classified into three neuronal cell types.
source: Morphologically, these DskGAL4 neurons could be classified into three neuronal types.
evidence: Supported by MCFO analysis shown in Figure 2D-G.

claim: Type I neurons project to the lobula and ventrolateral neuropils, and extend descending fibers to innervate the Accessory Mesothoracic Neuropil (AMNp) in the VNC.
source: The type I neurons project to the lobula and ventrolateral neuropils, and extend descending fibers to innervate the Accessory Mesothoracic Neuropil (AMNp) in the VNC (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by MCFO anatomical data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Type II neurons arborize in the ventrolateral neuropils and superior lateral protocerebrum.
source: The type II neurons arborize in the ventrolateral neuropils and superior lateral protocerebrum (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by MCFO anatomical data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The arborizations of type III neurons project ipsilaterally to the superior lateral protocerebrum.
source: The arborizations of type III neurons project ipsilaterally to the superior lateral protocerebrum (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by MCFO anatomical data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Male flies with DskGAL4 neurons inhibited by TNT showed reduced lunge frequency.
source: Compared to control males, male flies with DskGAL4 neurons inhibited by either TNT or Kir2.1 showed reduced lunge frequency and prolonged fighting latency (Figure 2H–K).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Male flies with DskGAL4 neurons inhibited by TNT showed prolonged fighting latency.
source: Compared to control males, male flies with DskGAL4 neurons inhibited by either TNT or Kir2.1 showed reduced lunge frequency and prolonged fighting latency (Figure 2H–K).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Male flies with DskGAL4 neurons inhibited by Kir2.1 showed reduced lunge frequency.
source: Compared to control males, male flies with DskGAL4 neurons inhibited by either TNT or Kir2.1 showed reduced lunge frequency and prolonged fighting latency (Figure 2H–K).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Male flies with DskGAL4 neurons inhibited by Kir2.1 showed prolonged fighting latency.
source: Compared to control males, male flies with DskGAL4 neurons inhibited by either TNT or Kir2.1 showed reduced lunge frequency and prolonged fighting latency (Figure 2H–K).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Males carrying DskGAL4 and UAS-dTRPA1 displayed higher aggression level at 28°C than at 21°C.
source: Males carrying DskGAL4 and UAS-dTRPA1 displayed higher aggression level at 28°C than at 21°C, and the temperature-dependent changes of aggression levels were not observed in males carrying DskGAL4 or UAS-dTRPA1 alone (Figure 2L–M; Video 2).
evidence: Supported by thermogenetic activation data shown in Figure 2L-M and Video 2.

claim: Temperature-dependent changes of aggression levels were not observed in males carrying DskGAL4 or UAS-dTRPA1 alone.
source: Males carrying DskGAL4 and UAS-dTRPA1 displayed higher aggression level at 28°C than at 21°C, and the temperature-dependent changes of aggression levels were not observed in males carrying DskGAL4 or UAS-dTRPA1 alone (Figure 2L–M; Video 2).
evidence: Supported by control experiments shown in Figure 2L-M.

claim: No significant changes of locomotion activity were observed after the inactivation or activation of DskGAL4 neurons.
source: In addition, no significant changes of locomotion activity were observed after the inactivation or activation of DskGAL4 neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by locomotion data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a negative correlation between the number of type I plus type II neurons inhibited and the lunge numbers of individual flies.
source: We found there is a negative correlation between the number of type I plus type II neurons inhibited and the lunge numbers of individual flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by mosaic analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Two putative Dsk receptors have been identified in Drosophila: CCKLR-17D1 and CCKLR-17D3.
source: Two putative Dsk receptors have been identified in Drosophila: CCKLR-17D1 and CCKLR-17D3 (Kubiak et al., 2002; Nässel and Williams, 2014; Nichols et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Aggressive behavior was largely abolished in ΔCCKLR-17D1 mutants compared with wildtype controls.
source: Aggressive behavior was largely abolished in ΔCCKLR-17D1 mutants compared with wildtype controls, while ΔCCKLR-17D3 mutants preserved normal level of aggression (Figure 3C and D), and no significant locomotion defects were observed for ΔCCKLR-17D1 and ΔCCKLR-17D3 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: ΔCCKLR-17D3 mutants preserved normal level of aggression.
source: Aggressive behavior was largely abolished in ΔCCKLR-17D1 mutants compared with wildtype controls, while ΔCCKLR-17D3 mutants preserved normal level of aggression (Figure 3C and D), and no significant locomotion defects were observed for ΔCCKLR-17D1 and ΔCCKLR-17D3 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: No significant locomotion defects were observed for ΔCCKLR-17D1 and ΔCCKLR-17D3 mutants.
source: Aggressive behavior was largely abolished in ΔCCKLR-17D1 mutants compared with wildtype controls, while ΔCCKLR-17D3 mutants preserved normal level of aggression (Figure 3C and D), and no significant locomotion defects were observed for ΔCCKLR-17D1 and ΔCCKLR-17D3 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by locomotion data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The reduced aggression phenotype in ΔCCKLR-17D1 mutants could be rescued by pan-neuronal expression of UAS-CCKLR-17D1 driven by elav-GAL4.
source: The reduced aggression phenotype could be rescued by pan-neuronal expression of UAS-CCKLR-17D1 driven by elav-GAL4 (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: RNAi silencing of CCKLR-17D1 using elav-GAL4 significantly suppressed aggression.
source: Moreover, RNAi silencing of CCKLR-17D1 using elav-GAL4 or CCKLR-17D1GAL4 also significantly suppressed aggression (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: RNAi silencing of CCKLR-17D1 using CCKLR-17D1GAL4 significantly suppressed aggression.
source: Moreover, RNAi silencing of CCKLR-17D1 using elav-GAL4 or CCKLR-17D1GAL4 also significantly suppressed aggression (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: CCKLR-17D1 is necessary for Dsk-mediated neuromodulation of aggressive behavior.
source: We conclude that CCKLR-17D1 is necessary for Dsk-mediated neuromodulation of aggressive behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that dTRPA1 activation of DskGAL4 neurons no longer enhanced aggression in the absence of CCKLR-17D1 (Figure 3G and H).

claim: dTRPA1 activation of DskGAL4 neuron no longer enhanced aggression level in the absence of CCKLR-17D1.
source: In this case, dTRPA1 activation of DskGAL4 neuron no longer enhanced aggression level in the absence of CCKLR-17D1 (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: Supported by behavioral epistasis data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: A subset of P1 neurons can promote aggression when activated.
source: Previous works revealed that several group of neurons including a subset of P1 neurons (Hoopfer et al., 2015), Fru– population of pC1 neurons (Koganezawa et al., 2016), pCd neurons (Jung et al., 2020), a small subset of aSP2 neurons (Watanabe et al., 2017), and a group of Fru+ Tk neurosn (Asahina et al., 2014) in the central brain can promote aggression when activated.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Hoopfer et al., 2015.

claim: Fru– population of pC1 neurons can promote aggression when activated.
source: Previous works revealed that several group of neurons including a subset of P1 neurons (Hoopfer et al., 2015), Fru– population of pC1 neurons (Koganezawa et al., 2016), pCd neurons (Jung et al., 2020), a small subset of aSP2 neurons (Watanabe et al., 2017), and a group of Fru+ Tk neurosn (Asahina et al., 2014) in the central brain can promote aggression when activated.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Koganezawa et al., 2016.

claim: pCd neurons can promote aggression when activated.
source: Previous works revealed that several group of neurons including a subset of P1 neurons (Hoopfer et al., 2015), Fru– population of pC1 neurons (Koganezawa et al., 2016), pCd neurons (Jung et al., 2020), a small subset of aSP2 neurons (Watanabe et al., 2017), and a group of Fru+ Tk neurosn (Asahina et al., 2014) in the central brain can promote aggression when activated.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jung et al., 2020.

claim: A small subset of aSP2 neurons can promote aggression when activated.
source: Previous works revealed that several group of neurons including a subset of P1 neurons (Hoopfer et al., 2015), Fru– population of pC1 neurons (Koganezawa et al., 2016), pCd neurons (Jung et al., 2020), a small subset of aSP2 neurons (Watanabe et al., 2017), and a group of Fru+ Tk neurosn (Asahina et al., 2014) in the central brain can promote aggression when activated.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Watanabe et al., 2017.

claim: A group of Fru+ Tk neurons can promote aggression when activated.
source: Previous works revealed that several group of neurons including a subset of P1 neurons (Hoopfer et al., 2015), Fru– population of pC1 neurons (Koganezawa et al., 2016), pCd neurons (Jung et al., 2020), a small subset of aSP2 neurons (Watanabe et al., 2017), and a group of Fru+ Tk neurosn (Asahina et al., 2014) in the central brain can promote aggression when activated.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Asahina et al., 2014.

claim: There might be direct connections between a subset of P1 neurons and Dsk-expressing neurons.
source: Our anterograde trans-synaptic tracing experiments using trans-Tango method (Talay et al., 2017) revealed that there might be direct connections between a subset of P1 neurons and Dsk-expressing neurons.
evidence: Supported by trans-Tango tracing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A few post-synaptic neurons showed immunoreactivity to Dsk, suggesting that these Dsk-expressing neurons are post-synaptic to a subset of P1 neurons.
source: Interestingly, a few post-synaptic neurons showed immunoreactivity to Dsk, suggesting that these Dsk-expressing neurons are post-synaptic to a subset of P1 neurons (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by trans-Tango tracing data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Significant GRASP signals were observed between R71G01-LexA labeled P1 neurons and DSK neurons.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed the connection between a subset of P1 neurons and Dsk-expressing neurons using the GFP Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners (GRASP) method (Alekseyenko et al., 2014; Feinberg et al., 2008). Significant GRASP signals were observed between R71G01-LexA labeled P1 neurons and DSK neurons (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Pan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A subset of P1 neurons axons overlap with DSK dendrites.
source: Moreover, Anatomical registration of a subset of P1 neurons and DSK neurons suggests that a subset of P1 neurons axons overlap with DSK dendrites (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by anatomical registration data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The aggression-promoting effect of activating a subset of P1 neurons is dramatically suppressed by the loss of the Dsk gene.
source: We observed that the aggression-promoting effect but not the courtship-promoting effect of a subset of P1 neurons activation is dramatically suppressed by the loss of the Dsk gene (Figure 4F and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral epistasis data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The courtship-promoting effect of a subset of P1 neurons activation is not suppressed by the loss of the Dsk gene.
source: We observed that the aggression-promoting effect but not the courtship-promoting effect of a subset of P1 neurons activation is dramatically suppressed by the loss of the Dsk gene (Figure 4F and G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by courtship behavior data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: ATP activation of P1 neurons elicited robust electrical responses from DSK-M neurons.
source: In perforate patch recordings, ATP activation of P1 neurons elicited robust electrical responses from DSK-M neurons and relatively weak responses from DSK-L neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ATP activation of P1 neurons elicited relatively weak responses from DSK-L neurons.
source: In perforate patch recordings, ATP activation of P1 neurons elicited robust electrical responses from DSK-M neurons and relatively weak responses from DSK-L neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ATP stimulation elicited a strong calcium response in DSK-M neurons.
source: Consistently, ATP stimulation elicited a strong calcium response in DSK-M neurons and a smaller calcium response in DSK-L neurons (Figure 5D and Video 3).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5D and Video 3.

claim: ATP stimulation elicited a smaller calcium response in DSK-L neurons.
source: Consistently, ATP stimulation elicited a strong calcium response in DSK-M neurons and a smaller calcium response in DSK-L neurons (Figure 5D and Video 3).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5D and Video 3.

claim: ATP activation of DSK neurons did not induce calcium responses in P1 neurons.
source: In contrast, ATP activation of DSK neurons did not induce calcium responses in P1 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dsk-expressing neurons receive inputs from P1 neurons.
source: These data further confirmed the functional connections between Dsk-expressing neurons and P1 neurons, suggesting that Dsk-expressing neurons receive inputs from P1 neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiology and calcium imaging data showing that P1 activation elicits responses in DSK neurons but not vice versa.

claim: Hierarchical relationships could be established during fly fighting: the winners dominate the food patch and maintain high levels of aggressiveness, while the losers retreat and exhibit reduced aggression.
source: It was well-known that hierarchical relationships could be established during fly fighting: the winners dominate the food patch and maintain high levels of aggressiveness, while the losers retreat and exhibit reduced aggression (Yurkovic et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Yurkovic et al., 2006.

claim: Conditional overexpression of Dsk can promote social dominance.
source: It suggests that conditional overexpression of Dsk can promote social dominance (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by social dominance experiments shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: The TRIC signals in the DSK-M neurons are significantly higher in the winner brains than in the loser and control brains.
source: We found that the TRIC signals in the DSK-M neurons are significantly higher in the winner brains than in the loser and control brains (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: Supported by TRIC data shown in Figure 6E-H.

claim: DSK-M neurons appear to be hyperactive in winners.
source: Thus DSK-M neurons appear to be hyperactive in winners.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TRIC data showing higher signals in winner brains.

claim: TRIC signals are not detectable in the DSK-L neurons.
source: It should be noted that TRIC signals are not detectable in the DSK-L neurons, possibly due to low levels of baseline activity in the DSK-L neurons.
evidence: This is an observation from the TRIC experiments.

claim: Low levels of baseline activity in the DSK-L neurons may explain why TRIC signals are not detectable in these neurons.
source: It should be noted that TRIC signals are not detectable in the DSK-L neurons, possibly due to low levels of baseline activity in the DSK-L neurons.
evidence: This is speculation about why TRIC signals are not detected in DSK-L neurons.

claim: Dsk is closely linked to the establishment of dominance.
source: Conditional overexpression of Dsk promotes winner effects, suggesting that Dsk is closely linked to the establishment of dominance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conditional overexpression and TRIC experiments.

claim: Cholecystokinin-like neuropeptide is likely to be evolutionarily conserved for the neuromodulation of aggression.
source: Taken together, our results elucidate the molecular and circuit mechanism underlying male aggression and suggest that cholecystokinin-like neuropeptide is likely to be evolutionarily conserved for the neuromodulation of aggression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between Dsk and CCK functions across species.

claim: The Dsk system acts downstream of a subset of P1 neurons specifically required for aggression.
source: This dissociation suggests that while a subset of P1 neurons signal an arousal state facilitating both aggression and courtship, the Dsk system acts downstream of a subset of P1 neurons specifically required for aggression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that loss of Dsk suppresses aggression but not courtship promoted by P1 activation.

claim: A subset of P1 neurons signal an arousal state facilitating both aggression and courtship.
source: This dissociation suggests that while a subset of P1 neurons signal an arousal state facilitating both aggression and courtship, the Dsk system acts downstream of a subset of P1 neurons specifically required for aggression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that P1 activation promotes both behaviors.

claim: Dsk is involved in feeding behavior.
source: As a caveat, it has been reported that Dsk is involved in feeding behavior (Nässel and Williams, 2014; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ΔDsk mutants show increased food consumption in the CAFE essay.
source: Our experiment also reproduced the result that ΔDsk mutants show increased food consumption in the CAFE essay (Diegelmann et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by feeding behavior data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the body size of flies and the aggression level.
source: Previous studies reported a positive correlation between the body size of flies and the aggression level, suggesting that the modulational effects of DSK neurons on aggression and feeding can be separated (Hoffmann, 1987; Hoffmann, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Hoffmann, 1987 and 1990.

claim: The modulational effects of DSK neurons on aggression and feeding can be separated.
source: Previous studies reported a positive correlation between the body size of flies and the aggression level, suggesting that the modulational effects of DSK neurons on aggression and feeding can be separated (Hoffmann, 1987; Hoffmann, 1990).
evidence: This is an inference based on previous studies showing correlation between body size and aggression.

claim: Type I and II neurons correspond to DSK-M.
source: Note that Type I and II neurons correspond to DSK-M and Type III neurons correspond to DSK-L.
evidence: This is a clarification of the relationship between the two classification systems.

claim: Type III neurons correspond to DSK-L.
source: Note that Type I and II neurons correspond to DSK-M and Type III neurons correspond to DSK-L.
evidence: This is a clarification of the relationship between the two classification systems.

claim: DSK-M neurons showed stronger responses to a subset of P1 neurons activation than DSK-L neurons.
source: Our finding that DSK-M neurons showed stronger responses to a subset of P1 neurons activation is consistent with the behavioral results of the flip-out experiment, in which Type I and II neurons, but not Type III, are critical to aggression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiology and calcium imaging data (Figure 5).

claim: Type I and II neurons, but not Type III, are critical to aggression.
